title: How Much Alcohol Is in a Shot? Ounces, ml and Standard Drinks
excerpt: A standard US shot is 1.5 oz of liquor. Here's how much pure alcohol that contains at every proof and pour size, how it compares to beer and wine, and why shots hit harder.
metaDescription: A standard shot is 1.5 oz (44 ml). See how much pure alcohol it holds at every proof and pour size, how it compares to beer and wine, and a simple formula.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how much alcohol is in a shot
content:
**The quick answer:** a standard US shot is **1.5 fluid ounces (about 44 ml)** of liquor. If that liquor is 80 proof (40% alcohol by volume, or ABV), the shot contains about **0.6 ounces, or 14 grams, of pure alcohol**. That is exactly one US "standard drink," the same amount of alcohol as a 12-ounce beer at 5% or a 5-ounce glass of wine at 12%.

That tidy answer falls apart fast in real life. Pours aren't always 1.5 ounces, shot glasses come in several sizes, and spirits range from sweet 15% liqueurs to 95% grain alcohol. This guide gives you the numbers for each case, a simple formula to work out any drink yourself, and the practical reasons shots tend to hit harder than the same alcohol in a beer.

> **A safety note before the numbers.** This page is for understanding what you're drinking, not for calculating whether you're safe to drive. Blood alcohol varies a lot between people, and you can be impaired well before you reach a legal limit. If you've been drinking, get a ride. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused and can't be woken, is vomiting while passed out, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, which is a medical emergency. Don't leave them to sleep it off.

## How Much Alcohol Is in a Standard Shot?

In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines one standard drink as any drink containing **0.6 fluid ounces, or about 14 grams, of pure alcohol**. A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof spirits was effectively used to set that benchmark, so the math lines up neatly:

- 1.5 oz of liquor x 40% alcohol = **0.6 oz of pure alcohol**
- In metric: 44.4 ml x 40% = 17.7 ml of pure alcohol
- Pure alcohol (ethanol) weighs about 0.79 grams per ml, so 17.7 ml x 0.79 = **about 14 grams**

So a "normal" shot of vodka, tequila, rum, gin, or whiskey bottled at 40% is one standard drink. Most mainstream bottles of those spirits in the US are sold at exactly 40%, which is why the 1.5-ounce shot is the reference pour that health agencies use.

### What "proof" and "ABV" mean

**ABV** is the percentage of the liquid that is pure alcohol. **Proof** is a US label term that is simply double the ABV. An 80-proof bottle is 40% ABV, 100 proof is 50% ABV, and 190 proof is 95% ABV. If a label gives only proof, divide by two to get the ABV you need for the math below.

## How Big Is a Shot? It Depends on Where You Are

There's no single worldwide size for a shot, and even inside the US the 1.5-ounce figure is a convention rather than a federal rule. Here are the common sizes you'll run into:

| Pour | Volume | Where you'll see it |
|---|---|---|
| Pony shot | 1 oz (about 30 ml) | Some bars, cocktail recipes |
| Standard US shot / jigger | 1.5 oz (about 44 ml) | The usual US bar pour and the basis of the US standard drink |
| "Tall" or generous shot | 2 oz (about 59 ml) | Many novelty shot glasses filled to the brim |
| Double | 3 oz (about 89 ml) | Doubles at US bars |
| UK single | 25 ml or 35 ml | UK pubs, which must use one of these legal measures for gin, rum, vodka, and whisky |
| Australian nip | 30 ml | Australian bars |
| Canadian shot | 1.5 oz (about 43 ml) | The basis of Canada's standard drink |

Two things to watch at home:

1. **Shot glasses vary.** Many glasses sold as "shot glasses" hold 2 ounces or more when filled to the top. Some have a fill line at 1 or 1.5 ounces, and many don't. If you've never measured yours, pour water from a measuring cup into it once and see.
2. **Free pours run large.** Bartenders using a jigger pour a consistent amount. People pouring at home, at parties, or from the bottle tend to pour more than they think, especially into big glasses. Studies that measure real-world home pours have repeatedly found that people overestimate how small their drinks are.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Different Shot Sizes?

Here's the same 80-proof (40% ABV) spirit poured into different shot sizes. "US standard drinks" assumes 14 grams of pure alcohol per drink.

| Shot size | Pure alcohol | US standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 oz (30 ml) | about 0.4 oz / 9.3 g | about 0.7 |
| 1.25 oz (37 ml) | about 0.5 oz / 11.7 g | about 0.8 |
| 1.5 oz (44 ml) | 0.6 oz / 14 g | 1.0 |
| 2 oz (59 ml) | 0.8 oz / 18.7 g | about 1.3 |
| 3 oz double (89 ml) | 1.2 oz / 28 g | 2.0 |
| UK 25 ml | about 7.9 g | about 0.6 (1 UK unit) |
| UK 35 ml | about 11 g | about 0.8 (1.4 UK units) |
| Australian 30 ml nip | about 9.5 g | about 0.7 (roughly 1 Australian standard drink) |

Notice that a "standard drink" isn't the same everywhere either. The US uses 14 grams. A UK **unit** is 8 grams (10 ml of pure alcohol), an Australian standard drink is 10 grams, and a Canadian standard drink is about 13.6 grams. So "one drink" in a UK or Australian guideline is a smaller amount of alcohol than "one drink" in a US guideline. If you read drinking advice from another country, keep that in mind.

## How Much Alcohol Is in a Shot by Proof?

The other big variable is how strong the liquor is. Here's a 1.5-ounce shot at different strengths:

| Strength | Typical examples | Pure alcohol per 1.5 oz | US standard drinks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15 to 17% (30 to 34 proof) | Cream liqueurs | about 0.23 to 0.26 oz | about 0.4 |
| 20% (40 proof) | Coffee liqueurs, many sweet liqueurs | 0.3 oz | 0.5 |
| 30% (60 proof) | Some flavored vodkas and schnapps | 0.45 oz | about 0.75 |
| 33 to 35% (66 to 70 proof) | Cinnamon whisky, herbal liqueurs | about 0.5 oz | about 0.85 |
| 40% (80 proof) | Most vodka, tequila, gin, rum, whiskey | 0.6 oz | 1.0 |
| 45% (90 proof) | Many bourbons and higher-strength gins | about 0.68 oz | about 1.1 |
| 50% (100 proof) | Bottled-in-bond whiskey, 100-proof vodka and schnapps | 0.75 oz | 1.25 |
| 55 to 65% (110 to 130 proof) | Barrel-proof and cask-strength whiskey | about 0.8 to 1.0 oz | about 1.4 to 1.6 |
| 75.5% (151 proof) | Overproof rum | about 1.1 oz | about 1.9 |
| 95% (190 proof) | Grain alcohol such as Everclear | about 1.4 oz | about 2.4 |

The two ends of this table are where people get caught out:

- **Liqueur shots** are weaker than they feel because they're sweet and easy to drink. But people tend to have more of them, so the total adds up.
- **High-proof shots** can be two or more standard drinks in a single swallow. One shot of 190-proof grain alcohol holds about as much alcohol as two and a half regular shots of vodka. Grain alcohol is meant to be diluted in mixed drinks, not taken straight, and drinking it neat also burns the mouth and throat.

Product strengths change by country and over time, and many brands make several versions. Some flavored "whisky" products sold in grocery and convenience stores are actually lower-strength malt or wine-based drinks with a similar name. Always check the ABV on the bottle in front of you.

## The Simple Formula for Any Drink

You don't need a chart if you remember one formula.

**In ounces (US):**
Ounces poured x ABV (as a decimal) / 0.6 = US standard drinks

Example: a 2-ounce pour of 100-proof bourbon is 2 x 0.50 / 0.6 = **about 1.7 standard drinks**.

**In milliliters:**
Milliliters poured x ABV (as a decimal) x 0.79 = grams of pure alcohol

Then divide by 14 for US standard drinks, by 8 for UK units, or by 10 for Australian standard drinks.

Example: a 35 ml pour of 40% gin is 35 x 0.40 x 0.79 = **about 11 grams**, which is 1.4 UK units or about 0.8 of a US standard drink.

The same formula works for beer and wine. A 16-ounce pint of 7% IPA is 16 x 0.07 / 0.6 = **about 1.9 standard drinks**, so that one craft beer has nearly as much alcohol as two shots.

## Shots vs Beer vs Wine: Same Alcohol, Different Effect

In a standard pour, the alcohol is equal:

| Drink | Typical pour | ABV | Pure alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liquor shot | 1.5 oz | 40% | 0.6 oz |
| Regular beer | 12 oz | 5% | 0.6 oz |
| Wine | 5 oz | 12% | 0.6 oz |
| Strong craft beer | 16 oz | 7 to 9% | about 1.1 to 1.4 oz |
| Restaurant wine pour | 6 to 9 oz | 13 to 14% | about 0.8 to 1.3 oz |

Your liver doesn't care whether the alcohol came from tequila or lager. Gram for gram, it is the same molecule, ethanol. But shots often feel stronger, and there are real reasons for that.

### Why shots tend to hit harder

1. **Speed.** A shot is finished in two seconds. A beer with the same alcohol might take 20 to 40 minutes. Taking the whole dose at once means your blood alcohol climbs faster and peaks higher. A 2014 study in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* that compared beer, wine, and spirits with matched doses of alcohol found that spirits produced the fastest rise and the highest peak blood alcohol of the three.
2. **Rounds stack up.** Shots tend to come in rounds, and rounds come on someone else's schedule. Your body clears very roughly one standard drink per hour. Four shots in an hour means about three are still waiting to be processed when the hour is up, and the effects keep rising for a while after the last one because alcohol is still being absorbed.
3. **The delay fools you.** It takes time for alcohol to move from your stomach and small intestine into your blood. If you judge how you feel 10 minutes after a round, you're judging only part of it. People often take the next shot before the last one has fully landed.
4. **Empty stomach.** Shots often happen before dinner, at pregames, or late at night after food has worn off. Food in the stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Without it, blood alcohol rises faster. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers which meals help most.
5. **Less water.** A beer is mostly water. A round of shots isn't, unless you add a glass of water yourself.

## How Much Alcohol Is in Mixed Drinks and Shooters?

Cocktails often contain more than one shot's worth of alcohol, and it's easy to lose count because you can't taste it.

- **A classic margarita** commonly uses 2 ounces of tequila plus an orange liqueur, which can come to roughly 1.5 to 2 standard drinks.
- **A martini** made with 2 to 3 ounces of gin or vodka and a little vermouth is often close to 2 standard drinks.
- **A Long Island iced tea** usually contains four or five different spirits. Even at half an ounce each, that's 2 to 2.5 ounces of liquor, or roughly 1.5 to 2 standard drinks, and many bars pour more.
- **Layered shooters and "bombs"** (a shot dropped into beer or an energy drink) combine a shot with another alcoholic drink, so one serving can be close to two standard drinks.
- **Jello shots** vary widely depending on the recipe. They're often weaker than a straight shot, but they're easy to eat a lot of quickly, and the alcohol is hard to judge.

Recipes vary so much that these are ranges, not exact numbers. The point is that a single cocktail is often more than one drink.

## What Counts as Moderate, and What Counts as Binge Drinking?

Knowing the alcohol in a shot is most useful when you match it to the guidance health agencies use.

- **Moderate drinking.** US dietary guidance has long described moderate drinking as up to 2 drinks a day for men and up to 1 for women, on days when people drink. In US terms, that's up to two 1.5-ounce shots of 80-proof liquor for men or one for women. Health agencies also say that drinking less is better for health than drinking more.
- **Binge drinking.** The NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings blood alcohol to 0.08% or higher, which for a typical adult is about **5 drinks for men or 4 for women in about 2 hours**. In shot terms, that's 4 or 5 regular shots in a couple of hours. Larger pours or stronger liquor get you there with fewer.

This is why shot counts can be misleading. "I had three shots" could mean three standard drinks, or it could mean five or six if the glasses were 2 ounces and the bottle was 100 proof.

## Do Shots Cause Worse Hangovers?

The biggest driver of a hangover is simply **how much alcohol you drank**, and shots make it easy to drink a lot quickly. Beyond the total amount, a few things matter:

- **Congeners.** These are by-products of fermentation and aging that give darker spirits their flavor. Bourbon, brandy, and other dark liquors contain more of them than vodka or gin. A 2010 study comparing bourbon and vodka at the same blood alcohol level found that people rated their hangovers somewhat worse after bourbon. The effect was modest, and the amount drunk mattered far more. Our [vodka hangover guide](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and [tequila hangover guide](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) go into how specific spirits compare.
- **Sugar and mixers.** Sweet shooters and syrupy mixers make it easier to drink more than you meant to, and very sugary drinks can add to nausea for some people.
- **Fast peaks and poor sleep.** A high blood alcohol late at night tends to disrupt the second half of sleep, which is a big part of why the next morning feels so bad.

There is no good evidence that any one type of liquor prevents hangovers. Fewer shots, slower pacing, food, and water do far more than switching brands. For the habits with the best support, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Practical Ways to Keep Track of Shots

If you want to enjoy a night out without losing count, these habits make the biggest difference:

1. **Know your pour.** At home, use a jigger or a measured shot glass. At a bar, it's fair to ask what size they pour.
2. **Check the proof.** Look at the label before the round. A 100-proof bottle is 25% stronger than an 80-proof one, and overproof rum or grain alcohol is about twice as strong or more.
3. **Count in standard drinks, not shots.** A 2-ounce shot is 1.3 drinks. A double is 2. Keep the running total honest.
4. **Space them out.** A shot every hour or so, with something non-alcoholic in between, keeps you much closer to the rate your body can handle than rounds every 10 minutes.
5. **Pair each shot with water.** It slows you down and keeps you from mistaking thirst for wanting another drink.
6. **Eat beforehand.** A real meal with protein, fat, and fiber slows the rise in blood alcohol.
7. **It's fine to skip a round.** Sipping a soda or water while others take a shot is common and rarely noticed.
8. **Plan your ride home before the first drink.** Never count shots to decide whether you can drive.

One more myth to drop: coffee, cold showers, and "walking it off" don't lower your blood alcohol. They might make you feel more alert, but only time clears the alcohol. If you're curious why, our explainer on [whether you can speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) walks through it.

## When Shots Turn Into an Emergency

Shots are one of the most common routes to alcohol poisoning because they deliver a large dose fast, and blood alcohol can keep rising after someone stops drinking or passes out.

> **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has been drinking:**
> - Is confused, very slow to respond, or can't be woken up
> - Is vomiting, especially while drowsy or passed out
> - Has slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or gaps of 10 seconds or more between breaths
> - Has a seizure
> - Has pale, bluish, or cold, clammy skin, or a low body temperature
>
> While you wait for help, stay with them. If they're lying down, roll them onto their side so they don't choke if they vomit. Don't give them coffee or a cold shower, and don't let them "sleep it off" alone. You don't need to see every sign before calling. In the US, Poison Control is also available at **1-800-222-1222**.

Many US states and colleges have Good Samaritan or medical amnesty policies that protect people who call for help in an alcohol emergency. Calling is always the right move.

If you notice you regularly can't stop at the number of shots you planned, or you're drinking in the morning to steady yourself, that's worth a conversation with a doctor. They can help without judgment.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people who drink socially take a DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplement on nights out. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied mainly in animals and lab models for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with limited human data so far. It's promising, but it's no substitute for pacing yourself.

To be clear about the limits: **there is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol, makes you less impaired, or makes it safe to drive.** It doesn't change how much alcohol is in a shot or how quickly your body clears it. If you'd like to try it as one part of a sensible plan that still includes food, water, and fewer shots, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- A standard US shot is **1.5 ounces (about 44 ml)**. At 80 proof, it contains **0.6 ounces or 14 grams of pure alcohol**, which is one standard drink.
- The real amount depends on the **pour size** (1 to 3 ounces is common) and the **proof** (from about 15% for cream liqueurs to 95% for grain alcohol).
- To work it out yourself: **ounces x ABV / 0.6 = US standard drinks.**
- A shot has the same alcohol as a regular beer or a glass of wine, but it goes down in seconds, so blood alcohol rises faster and higher.
- Count in standard drinks, space shots out, eat first, drink water, and never use a shot count to decide whether you can drive.
- If someone can't be woken, is vomiting while passed out, or is breathing slowly after drinking, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many ounces or milliliters are in a shot?**

In the US, a standard shot is 1.5 fluid ounces, which is about 44 ml. There's no single federal law that fixes the size of a shot, so some bars pour 1 ounce or 1.25 ounces, and many shot glasses hold 2 ounces when filled to the brim. In the UK, legal spirit measures are 25 ml or 35 ml, and in Australia a standard nip is 30 ml.

**Is one shot equal to one standard drink?**

Only if it's a 1.5-ounce shot of an 80-proof (40% ABV) spirit. That pour holds about 0.6 ounces, or 14 grams, of pure alcohol, which is exactly one US standard drink. A bigger pour, a stronger spirit, or a double counts as more than one drink. A shot of a 20% liqueur is closer to half a drink.

**How much pure alcohol is in a shot of vodka, tequila, or whiskey?**

Most vodka, tequila, gin, rum, and whiskey is sold at 40% ABV (80 proof). A 1.5-ounce shot of any of them contains about 0.6 ounces (roughly 17.7 ml, or 14 grams) of pure alcohol. Higher-proof bottles contain more: a 100-proof shot has about 0.75 ounces, or 1.25 standard drinks.

**Is a shot stronger than a beer?**

Not if you compare standard sizes. A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor, a 12-ounce beer at 5%, and a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine each contain about the same amount of alcohol. The difference is speed: a shot goes down in seconds, so your blood alcohol rises faster than it does when you sip a beer over half an hour. Strong craft beers in pint glasses can also hold more alcohol than a single shot.

**How many shots are in a bottle of liquor?**

A standard 750 ml bottle (a 'fifth') holds about 17 shots of 1.5 ounces. A 1-liter bottle holds about 22, and a 1.75-liter 'handle' holds about 39. A 50 ml mini bottle is roughly 1.7 ounces, a little more than one standard shot.

**How long does it take for one shot to leave your system?**

As a rough guide, the liver clears about one standard drink per hour, so one 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor takes around an hour or a bit more to process. The real rate varies with body size, sex, liver health, food, and genetics. Nothing you can drink or take, including coffee, water, or supplements, speeds this up in any meaningful way.

**How many shots does it take to get drunk or reach the legal limit?**

There's no safe number to rely on. Blood alcohol depends on your weight, sex, how fast you drink, whether you've eaten, and how quickly your body processes alcohol. As a reference point, the NIAAA defines binge drinking as about 4 drinks for women or 5 for men in around 2 hours, which typically brings blood alcohol to 0.08%, the US driving limit. Many people are impaired well below that. If you're drinking, don't drive.

**How many calories are in a shot?**

A 1.5-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor has roughly 95 to 100 calories, nearly all from the alcohol itself (about 7 calories per gram). Sweet liqueurs and flavored spirits add sugar on top of that, and mixers and chasers add more.
